question: The word 'robot' comes from an old word for forced labour, the work peasants owed their lords. Which European language gave the world 'robot'?
source_excerpt: Traditionally, a robota was the period of work a serf owed his lord, typically six months a year.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a word this futuristic must come from English science fiction or Latin technical jargon. In fact it comes from a Central European language and literally means grinding serf labour, which reframes every robot as an overworked servant.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 'robot' derives from Czech 'robota' (forced labour owed by serfs), popularized by Čapek's R.U.R.

explanation: Writer Karel Čapek used it in his 1920 play R.U.R., on his brother Josef's suggestion, from 'robota', meaning drudgery or compulsory labour. So every robot is, by name, a serf.

question: Ketchup's name comes from a sauce sold in southern China centuries ago, but that original sauce had no tomatoes in it. What was it made from?
source_excerpt: brine of pickled fish or shell-fish

extra.why_interesting: Everyone takes tomato as the very definition of ketchup. The original sauce behind the word had no tomato at all and was a salty fermented fish brine, closer to fish sauce than to anything on a burger.
extra.verification_notes: Standard Hokkien kê-chiap etymology is a fish brine/fish sauce; Wikipedia notes the etymology is not fully settled (Malay kicap theory), but the answer fits the mainstream account (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketchup).

explanation: The Hokkien 'kê-tsiap' was a salty fish brine. European traders took the name home, tried versions with mushrooms and walnuts, and Americans only settled on tomato in the 1800s.
